newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian markets stabilise after currency jolts.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian markets stabilise after currency jolts.

text.p: Indonesian financial markets calmed on Tuesday after being jolted by recent currency volatility in the region, analysts said.

The rupiah recovered to 2,450 per U.S. dollar at 1015 GMT from 2,453.0 at the opening and 2,469 on Monday. Speculative attacks on the rupiah escalated early this week following the recent de facto devaluations of the Thai and Philippine currencies.
The stock market also found support, with the composite index of 266 companies closing little changed at 722.21 points after sliding sharply in the past two trading days.
Currency dealers remained cautious, saying speculative attacks on other currencies in the region had not yet ceased and the rupiah could be hit by further turbulence.
However, analysts expressed confidence in the rupiah and said they had not revised their earnings forecasts for Indonesian companies.
"The rupiah is traded back below (the) 2,450 level, so I think that is a good sign that the market is finding its own level," an analyst with a U.S. investment bank in Singapore said.
The analyst said concerns were now focused more on the Malaysian ringgit.
"The rupiah is one of the currencies that we are comfortable with, especially in the long term. It's not a currency that we are looking at in term of risks," he said.

Indonesia's central Bank Indonesia governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television in Tokyo that the bank's widening of the dollar-rupiah band last Friday had been a pre-emptive move as speculators hit the Thai and Philippine currencies and attacked the Malaysian ringgit.
He said the central bank would continue its policy of a steady depreciation of the rupiah against the dollar, currently at four to five percent a year.
Instability in the currency market, coupled with profit-taking after several record highs in the wake of an economic deregulation package, caused some corrections in the stock market.
Stephanus Partono, an analyst with Goldman Sachs, told Reuters Indonesia was one of the beneficiaries from recent fund flows into the region because of its sound economic fundamentals.

"There was some shift of funds into Indonesia recently which boosted the market. But because of currency concerns, investors are cutting their exposures in Asian stocks, including Indonesia," Partono said.
Partono said foreign investors were adopting a cautious stance following currency instability in Southeast Asian countries.
But Goldman had not changed its assumption.

"We still forecast a four to five percent rupiah depreciation this year. Therefore, we don't feel it's time to revise our earnings forecast for Indonesia," Partono said, adding that Goldmans expected earnings per share growth for 1997 at 16.0 percent.
Bond dealers said fixed income investors were nervous on Monday following the currency turmoil, but said they seemed to have calmed on Tuesday and were holding back from unloading.
The U.S. investment bank analyst said he was not advising clients to stay away from the rupiah market, but given the current volatility it made sense to be cautious.
"The market is nervous. In a nervous situation people will not pay attention so much to fundamental valuation," he said.
"In fact if you look at what is happening in the rupiah, you can see there is a lot of stability there. It's a very good sign that the market is not panicking," the analyst said.
